name: Python Programming
description: Writing clear, idiomatic Python using core data types, control flow, functions and the standard library.

questions.question: What does len([1, 2, [3, 4]]) return?
questions.explanation: The outer list has three elements: 1, 2 and the nested list [3, 4]. len() does not count elements of nested lists.

questions.question: Which keyword starts a named function definition in Python?
questions.explanation: Named functions are defined with the def keyword, e.g. def greet(name):.

questions.question: What is printed by: x = [1, 2, 3]; y = x; y.append(4); print(x)
questions.explanation: Assignment binds y to the same list object as x, so mutating it through y is visible through x.

questions.question: Which of these built-in types is immutable?
questions.explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation; lists, dicts and sets can be modified in place.

questions.question: Given def f(a, lst=[]): lst.append(a); return lst — what does print(f(2)) output if f(1) was called once before?
questions.explanation: Default argument values are evaluated once at definition time, so the same list is shared across calls and keeps the 1 from the first call.

questions.question: What does sum(x * x for x in range(10**6)) avoid compared to sum([x * x for x in range(10**6)])?
options: Building the whole intermediate list in memory
questions.explanation: A generator expression yields values lazily one at a time, so no million-element list is materialised; the result is the same.

practical.title: Word frequency counter
practical.instructions: Write a Python function count_words(text) that returns a dictionary mapping each lowercase word to the number of times it appears. Split words on whitespace.
practical.expected_output: A function named count_words that lowercases the text, splits it on whitespace, counts occurrences (with a dict, dict.get, defaultdict or collections.Counter) and returns the result.

rubric.hint: Use text.lower() so 'The' and 'the' count as the same word.
Increment a count per word, e.g. counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1, or use collections.Counter.
The function should return the dictionary, not just print it.

tasks.title: Work through the official Python tutorial basics
tasks.description: Read sections 3 to 5 of the official Python tutorial (informal introduction, control flow, data structures). Type and run every example in an interpreter rather than just reading.
tasks.completion_criteria: You can write a loop, a function and use lists and dicts without looking up syntax.

tasks.title: Solve 10 small Python exercises
tasks.description: Write 10 short scripts such as FizzBuzz, reversing a string, finding the max of a list without max(), and counting vowels. Run each with a few inputs to confirm it works.
tasks.completion_criteria: 10 working scripts saved in a folder, each tested with at least 2 inputs.

tasks.title: Use the standard library for file and data processing
tasks.description: Write a script that reads a CSV file with the csv module, aggregates a column with collections.Counter or defaultdict, and writes a summary to a new file. Use functions and a main guard.
tasks.completion_criteria: Script runs from the command line on a sample CSV and produces a correct summary file.

tasks.title: Build a command-line tool
tasks.description: Build a small CLI (for example a to-do manager or expense tracker) using argparse, JSON file storage and separate modules. Include error handling for bad input and missing files.
tasks.completion_criteria: Tool supports at least 3 subcommands, persists data between runs and handles invalid input without crashing.
